newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Regent Fund backs down to Gazprom pressure.
newsitem.headline: Regent Fund backs down to Gazprom pressure.

text.p: A big international fund company has backed down from plans to invest in the domestic shares of Russian gas monopoly Gazprom in the face of intense opposition from the powerful corporation.

Moscow share traders and analysts said the Regent Fund would have been unwise to fight Gazprom, the world's largest gas company, which numbers Russia's current prime minister and energy minister among its former executives.

Regent Gaz Investment had been planning to take advantage of the fact that internationally traded shares in Gazprom, quoted in the form of American Depositary Shares in London, cost about four times as much as Gazprom's shares in Russia.
But Regent Gaz Investment Co Ltd said in a statement issued at the weekend that it would not proceed with plans to invest in Gazprom shares.
"The Board has taken this decision with regret as we continue to believe that our strategy to help passive investors participate in RAO Gazprom's success was appropriate and legal," the fund said.
Regent Gaz Investment Co Ltd is managed by Regent Fund Management, part of Hong Kong based Regent Pacific Group.
Neil Greer, chief executive of Regent European Securities, Moscow, another member of the Regent group, was unavailable for comment.

Gazprom said last Monday it had written to Regent Fund Management asking it to stop the off-shore fund from investing in domestic Gazprom shares. Analysts and traders said the price of the ADSs could have been hurt by the Regent scheme.
Gazprom said the scheme was contrary to Russian law and Gazprom's own rules, although Regent said it had been advised the scheme was legal.

Gazprom rules make it difficult to trade the domestic shares, which is why foreign investors have been willing to pay a premium for the ADSs. Gazprom also wants to limit the amount of its shares in foreign hands for national security reasons.
Russia's securities watchdog, the Federal Commission on the Securities Market, has not commented officially on the dispute.
"I can only imagine it didn't go through because they got such a bad response from Gazprom," said Kristen Staples, Director of Communications and Public Affairs.
Moscow brokerage houses were not surprised by the fund's decision to back away.

"Gazprom has always been a very closed company, not very friendly to outsiders," said Chris Smart, director of research at Pioneer Securities. "Because of its size and weight in the market it has been able to make up rules for itself."
Gleb Shestakov, managing director of Global Fund Management, Moscow, said Regent had backed down for diplomatic rather than legal reasons.
"It would have been a very bad idea for Regent to start fighting Gazprom in the courts," he said.
Gazprom shares rose on Monday to $0.530 from $0.512 on Friday. Gazprom ADSs, equivalent to 10 underlying shares, were $20.600 in London after closing on Friday at $20.005.
